<header class="dg-head dg-head-chapter"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 6</p><h1 class="dg-title">Covariant Derivative</h1></header>
<div class="dg-motivation"><div class="dg-motivation-title">Motivation: Differentiating vector fields</div><div class="dg-motivation-upper"><p>A vector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\)</span> already differentiates scalar fields, <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}\left\lfloor f \right\rceil\)</span> being the directional derivative of <span class="math inline">\(f\)</span> (Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/vector-fields.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Vector_Fields">5.1</a>). Differentiating a vector field <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}\)</span> along <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p\)</span> is harder. A difference quotient along a curve through <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span> would subtract <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}_{\gamma(\lambda)} \in T_{\gamma(\lambda)}\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}_p \in T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>, which live in different vector spaces. Differentiating the components does not work either, because the result depends on the chart. With <span class="math inline">\(\left. \mathcal{Y} \right|_\mathcal{U} = \tilde{x}^j \, \partial x_j\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p = x^i_p \, (\partial x_i)_p\)</span>, and components <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{y}^k = \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \, \tilde{x}^j\)</span> in a second chart (Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../fields/tensor-fields-and-notation.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_Tensor_Fields_and_notation">5.3</a>),  <span class="math display">\[
        \mathcal{X}_p(\tilde{y}^k)
        \overset{\text{product rule}}{=}
        \underbrace{\left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p \mathcal{X}_p(\tilde{x}^j)}_{\text{transformation law of a vector}}
        + \underbrace{\tilde{x}^j(p) \, x^i_p \; \partial_i \partial_j \left[ \mathscr{Y}^k \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right] \big( \mathscr{X}(p) \big)}_{\text{second derivatives of the chart transition map}} .
    \]</span>  The second term vanishes for all <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{Y}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p\)</span> only if the chart transition map is affine, so the numbers <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{X}_p(\tilde{x}^j)\)</span> are not the components of a vector.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>Comparing tangent vectors at different points therefore requires an additional structure.</p>
</div><div class="dg-motivation-lower">
<p><strong>Goal.</strong> Define this structure and the tensors that characterize it.</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>A <strong>connection</strong> <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span> is the rule for differentiating tensor fields along a tangent vector. In a chart it is encoded in the connection coefficient functions <span class="math inline">\(\Gamma_\mathscr{X}\)</span>, whose transformation law contains the second-derivative term above.</p></li>
<li><p>Differentiating along curves defines <strong>parallel transport</strong> and the straight curves of <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>, its <strong>autoparallels</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p>The <strong>torsion</strong> and the <strong>Riemann curvature</strong> characterize <span class="math inline">\(\nabla\)</span>. The curvature measures the path dependence of parallel transport.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>In Newton–Cartan theory and in general relativity, free particles move along autoparallels and gravity is encoded in the connection. The part of gravity that no choice of chart removes is the curvature.</p></div></div>
